name: Inosine
short: Kidney stones: 7.0 per 100 patient-years on oral inosine vs 1.4 on placebo in a 298-person early Parkinson trial; stones in 2 smaller trials, 1 a severe event. Inosine raises serum urate.
text: Inosine is a urate precursor, and in trials it raised serum urate, by about 2 mg/dL in a phase 3 trial of oral inosine in 298 people with early Parkinson disease treated for up to 2 years. In that trial, people taking inosine had more kidney stones than those on placebo (7.0 vs 1.4 stones per 100 patient-years) but fewer serious adverse events (7.4 vs 13.1 per 100 patient-years), and the trial was stopped early for futility; its authors noted that urate elevation is associated with crystal-related, cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. In an earlier dose-ranging trial in 75 people with early Parkinson disease, serious adverse events were no more common with inosine than with placebo, no one developed gout, and 3 people taking inosine developed symptomatic urinary stones. In a 20-week trial in 23 people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (14 on inosine), overall adverse events were similar to placebo, but renal adverse events occurred in 3 people taking inosine, hypertension in 1, and 2 had kidney stones judged to be related to treatment, one of them severe. In a 6-month trial in 120 postmenopausal women, inosine raised serum urate without significant differences in blood pressure, lipids or overall kidney function, although estimated kidney function was lower with inosine at week 13. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
